results.summary_before: This is an implementation of the classic SIMON memory game, where the user must repeat an ever-growing sequence of button presses. It uses four buttons for input and a 7-segment display to show the current sequence length or an 'L' upon losing. The design requires a Digilent PmodBTN for button input and has been tested successfully by multiple users. It is a simple, self-contained game with no additional external hardware beyond the Pmod.

results.summary_before: This design implements the 2048 sliding tile puzzle game with VGA output. The player uses four buttons to move tiles in four directions, merging matching numbers to reach 2048. It includes a debug mode for unit testing and requires a TinyVGA Pmod for display. Silicon testing confirmed it works, with a tester successfully playing a game.

results.summary_before: Warp is a demoscene-style graphics and audio demo written in the Silice HDL, outputting VGA color and sync signals plus an audio pin. It is intended to be run with a VGA PMOD and an audio PMOD attached to the Tiny Tapeout board, and the same design was simulated on an ECPIX5 with those PMODs and on an ULX3S using its DAC for audio only. Silicon test reports from two independent testers confirm that both graphics and audio work as expected, and the author notes the design was updated in January 2026 to confirm ASIC operation. It is notable as a demonstration of the Silice HDL and as an entry in the Tiny Tapeout demoscene competition.

results.summary_before: This design is the digital block from a larger VGA project, packaged with a simple sequencer loop and dithering to simulate 8-bit color output on the 2-bit Tiny VGA Pmod. It runs standalone by plugging into a VGA monitor and resetting, with manual mode and bit-depth selection available by overriding the sequencer. It requires a Tiny VGA Pmod and a 25 MHz clock, and silicon tests by the author confirm it works as expected. The design is a 1x1 tile implementation intended for the Tiny Tapeout shuttle.

results.summary_before: This is the same digital VGA block as the Tiny VGA version but targeting the Digilent PmodVGA with 4 bits per color channel, including a simple sequencer loop and dithering. It runs standalone when connected to a VGA monitor and reset, with manual mode and bit-depth selection possible by overriding the sequencer. It requires a Digilent PmodVGA and a 25 MHz clock, and the author's silicon test confirms it works as expected. The documentation notes that another version of this design on the same shuttle targets the Tiny VGA Pmod.

results.summary_before: This design drives a 7-segment display to show the text PILIPINASLASALLE one character per clock cycle, with the decimal point toggling each cycle. It also has a manual mode where a 4-bit BCD input selects which character to display. It is based on a Wokwi project and requires an external 7-segment display. Silicon tests confirm it works in default mode, and a second tester verified both modes, noting that a slow clock is needed and the demoboard clock button is poorly debounced.
